lessons.title: Wheezing children: grading how bad it really is
lessons.body:
Two wheezing children can look identical from the doorway and need opposite things. Age and history sort them out. After that, the only question left is how far down the road this child has already walked.

## Why a small airway is a big problem

Airway resistance depends on the radius raised to the fourth power. Halve the inside diameter of a tube and resistance goes up about `16` times. A toddler's bronchiole is already narrow, so `1 mm` of swelling does far more damage than the same `1 mm` in an adult.

**Asthma** is three problems stacked: muscle squeezing the airway shut (bronchospasm), swelling of the lining, and thick mucus plugging what is left. Albuterol relaxes only the muscle. That is why a child can still be working hard after a perfect treatment.

**Bronchiolitis** is a virus, usually RSV, that inflames and plugs the smallest airways of a child under `2`. It peaks at `3 to 6 months` of age and between November and March. Because it is plugging rather than spasm, albuterol often changes nothing.

| | Bronchiolitis | Asthma |
|---|---|---|
| Age | Under `2`, most under `12 months` | Usually over `2` |
| History | First or second episode, sick contacts | Repeat attacks, inhaler at home, triggers |
| Onset | `2 to 3 days` of runny nose, then wheeze | Hours, often after a trigger |
| Sounds | Wheezes plus wet crackles | Dry wheeze |
| Albuterol | Often no change | Usually helps |

## Grading an asthma attack

Grade by what the child can do, not by how loud the wheeze is.

- **Mild:** speaks in full sentences, sits normally, wheeze only at the end of exhaling, SpO2 `94%` or higher.
- **Moderate:** speaks in short phrases, wants to sit up, wheeze through all of exhaling, obvious retractions and nasal flaring, SpO2 `90 to 94%`.
- **Severe:** single words only, sits forward and refuses to lie down, wheeze both in and out, deep retractions, SpO2 under `90%`, heart rate high for age.
- **Failing:** quiet chest, drowsy or agitated then flat, poor effort, cyanosis, slowing heart rate.

> **Trap:** A chest that has gone quiet in a child who is still working hard is the worst finding in pediatrics. Air that does not move makes no sound. That child gets ventilated, not reassured.

The second silent warning is a respiratory rate that falls while the child gets no better. A tiring child slows down. Rate falling plus effort falling plus rising drowsiness is respiratory failure in progress.

## What you actually do

Leave the child where they are calmest, usually upright on a caregiver. Oxygen to keep SpO2 `94%` or higher, blow-by if a mask starts a fight, because a screaming child moves less air than a calm one.

For asthma, assist with the child's own inhaler or give nebulized albuterol per protocol: `2.5 mg` in `3 mL` at `6 to 8 L/min`, or `1.25 mg` in the youngest children in some systems. A metered-dose inhaler with a spacer delivers `90 mcg` per puff, usually `2` puffs, and with a spacer and mask it works as well as a nebulizer for mild and moderate attacks. Severe attacks get back-to-back treatments where protocol allows.

For bronchiolitis, the highest-yield thing you will do all call is **suction the nose**. Infants under about `4 months` depend on nasal breathing. Then oxygen, head elevated, and two questions: how much is the baby feeding, and how many wet diapers? Under half the usual feeds, or fewer than `4` wet diapers in `24 hours`, means dehydration on top of the illness.

> **Key:** Any infant under `2 months` with bronchiolitis can simply stop breathing, even with lungs that sound fine. Those babies are transported and watched, every time.

If you have to ventilate a wheezing child, bag slowly and let the chest fall all the way between breaths. These children trap air, and stacking breaths raises pressure in the chest until blood pressure drops.
keyPoints: Grade asthma by speech: sentences is mild, phrases is moderate, single words is severe, silence is failure.
A quiet chest with continued effort, or a falling respiratory rate with rising drowsiness, is impending arrest.
Albuterol 2.5 mg in 3 mL nebulized at 6 to 8 L/min, or 2 puffs of 90 mcg by MDI with a spacer.
Bronchiolitis is plugging, not spasm: suction the nose first, expect little from albuterol, and watch infants under 2 months for apnea.
Bag slowly and allow full exhalation in a wheezing child to avoid air trapping and a falling blood pressure.

checks.q: A 6-year-old has been wheezing loudly for 30 minutes. After a nebulizer his wheeze is much quieter, but he is now drowsy with a respiratory rate that dropped from 44 to 20 and SpO2 of 89%. What is happening?
choices: He is improving and can be monitored during a routine transport
He is tiring and moving almost no air, and needs assisted ventilation
The albuterol caused sedation and should be stopped
The pulse oximeter is reading a poor waveform
checks.why: A quieter chest with a falling rate, falling effort and rising drowsiness is respiratory failure, not improvement. Air that is not moving cannot wheeze. Assist ventilations and call for ALS.

checks.q: A 7-month-old in February has had three days of runny nose and now wheezes with fine crackles. This is his first episode. What is the highest-yield first intervention?
choices: Nebulized albuterol
An epinephrine auto-injector
Suction the nose and give oxygen with the head elevated
Lay him flat to auscultate all lung fields
checks.why: This is bronchiolitis, which plugs airways rather than causing spasm, so albuterol often does nothing. Infants breathe through the nose, so nasal suctioning is the intervention that changes his work of breathing.

checks.q: Why must you ventilate a severe asthmatic slowly with full exhalation time?
choices: Because fast ventilation causes vomiting
Because they trap air, and stacking breaths raises chest pressure and drops blood pressure
Because albuterol makes the lungs stiff
Because slow breaths deliver more oxygen per breath
checks.why: Obstructed airways empty slowly. If you give the next breath before the last one is out, pressure builds in the chest, venous return falls, and the blood pressure crashes.

lessons.title: Stridor, tracheitis and the choking child
lessons.body:
Noise tells you where the problem is. Snoring is the tongue. **Stridor**, a harsh crowing sound on breathing in, is the voice box or just below it. Wheezing on the way out is deep in the chest. A child with stridor has a narrowed upper airway, and your job is to decide which narrowing it is without making it worse.

## The stridor differential

| Condition | Age | Fever | Onset | Tell |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Croup | `6 months to 3 years` | Low | `1 to 2 days`, worse at night | Barking cough, better in cool air |
| Epiglottitis | Classically `3 to 7 years` | High | Hours | Drooling, tripod, muffled voice, no cough |
| Bacterial tracheitis | `3 to 8 years` | High | Croup for days, then sudden decline | Barky cough plus a toxic look |
| Foreign body | `1 to 4 years` | None | Seconds | Witnessed choking, no illness before it |
| Anaphylaxis | Any | None | Minutes | Hives, swelling, vomiting, an exposure |
| Retropharyngeal abscess | Under `6 years` | High | Days | Neck held rigid, refuses to move it |

**Bacterial tracheitis** is the one nobody warns you about. A child has croup, plateaus or briefly improves, then over a few hours spikes a fever, looks genuinely sick, and the stridor worsens instead of easing. Thick pus lines the trachea and can peel loose and block it. It does not respond to the nebulized epinephrine that fixes croup, and it is managed in an operating room. Handle it like epiglottitis: hands off the throat, oxygen, calm, fast.

> **Key:** Croup that is getting worse with a high fever and a toxic-looking child is not croup any more.

## Croup you can grade

- **Mild:** barky cough, stridor only when upset, no retractions at rest.
- **Moderate:** stridor at rest with retractions, still interactive.
- **Severe:** stridor at rest, deep retractions, agitation or lethargy, pale or dusky.

Field care is deliberately gentle: leave the child on a caregiver, blow-by oxygen only if needed, cool outside air often helps on the way to the truck, and do not start procedures that make them cry. The hospital gives dexamethasone `0.6 mg/kg` and nebulized epinephrine for stridor at rest. Some systems carry nebulized epinephrine at the BLS level — varies by protocol.

## The choking child

Airway obstruction is a leading cause of death under `4`. The worst offenders are round and compressible: hot dog pieces, whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, hard candy. Non-food classics are coins, marbles, small toy parts, and **button batteries**, which burn through tissue in as little as `2 hours` and are an emergency even when breathing is normal.

Decide by air exchange, not by how frightened the room is.

**Good air exchange** means a forceful cough, crying, speech, pink skin. Do nothing but let them cough. Stay close, offer oxygen if tolerated, position of comfort, transport. Slapping the back of a child with a partial obstruction can convert it to a complete one.

**Poor or no air exchange** means a silent cough, no sound at all, cyanosis, or a thin high-pitched squeak:

1. **Under `1 year`:** `5` back slaps between the shoulder blades with the head lower than the body, then `5` chest thrusts on the lower half of the sternum with two fingers. Repeat. No abdominal thrusts — the infant liver is exposed.
2. **`1 year` and older:** abdominal thrusts from behind, fist above the navel and below the ribs, until the object comes out or the child goes limp.
3. **Unresponsive:** lower them to the floor and start **CPR**, beginning with compressions. Each time you open the airway for a breath, look in the mouth and remove the object only if you can see it. Compressions generate higher airway pressure than back slaps do.

> **Trap:** Never sweep a finger blindly through a child's mouth. You will push a wedged object past the cords and turn a partial obstruction into a complete one.

An object that already dropped past the cords settles in one bronchus, usually the right. Days later the child has a lingering cough and a wheeze on one side only. A one-sided wheeze in a toddler is a foreign body until a bronchoscopy proves otherwise.
keyPoints: Stridor is upper airway; grade croup by whether stridor is present at rest and whether there are retractions.
Bacterial tracheitis is croup that worsens with high fever and a toxic child, and it does not respond to nebulized epinephrine.
Good air exchange means encourage coughing and transport; slapping a partial obstruction can make it complete.
Infants get 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts, children 1 year and older get abdominal thrusts, and an unresponsive choking patient gets CPR.
Never perform a blind finger sweep; look before every rescue breath and remove only what you can see.

checks.q: A 4-year-old had a barking cough for two days. Tonight he has a temperature of 103.5 F, looks toxic, and his stridor is worse despite nebulized epinephrine at the urgent care. What is most likely?
choices: Worsening viral croup
Bacterial tracheitis
Asthma
Retropharyngeal abscess
checks.why: Croup that deteriorates with a high fever, a toxic appearance, and no response to nebulized epinephrine is bacterial tracheitis. It is an airway emergency managed in an operating room.

checks.q: A 2-year-old choked on a peanut and is coughing forcefully, crying, and pink. What do you do?
choices: Five abdominal thrusts immediately
Back blows until the peanut comes out
Encourage coughing, keep her in a position of comfort, give oxygen and transport
Perform a finger sweep to feel for the peanut
checks.why: Forceful coughing and crying mean good air exchange and a partial obstruction. Intervening can dislodge the object into a worse position. Watch closely, because silence means it has become complete.

lessons.title: Pediatric shock and dehydration by the numbers
lessons.body:
A child's blood pressure is the last thing to fail and the first thing people look at. Everything useful happens before it moves.

## How much volume is actually there

Children carry about `75 mL/kg` of blood, an infant closer to `80 mL/kg`, an adult about `70 mL/kg`. Multiply it out and the fragility becomes obvious.

| Child | Weight | Total blood volume | A 20% loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn | `3.5 kg` | about `280 mL` | `56 mL` |
| 1-year-old | `10 kg` | about `800 mL` | `160 mL` |
| 5-year-old | `20 kg` | about `1,500 mL` | `300 mL` |
| 10-year-old | `32 kg` | about `2,400 mL` | `480 mL` |

A soda can of blood is roughly a quarter of a toddler's supply. That is why scalp lacerations and femur fractures matter so much more in children, and why a puddle that looks small is not.

## Heart rate is the only lever they have

Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. A young child's heart cannot meaningfully increase stroke volume, so the only way to raise output is to beat faster and squeeze the vessels tighter. Tachycardia plus cool, mottled skin with delayed capillary refill is the entire compensation strategy, and it shows up long before the pressure moves.

**Compensated shock:** fast heart rate, cool pale or mottled skin, capillary refill over `2 seconds`, weak peripheral pulses with a strong central pulse, anxious or fussy, normal blood pressure.

**Decompensated shock:** all of that plus a systolic pressure under `70 plus twice the age in years`, a weak central pulse, and a child who has gone quiet. Under `1 year` the floor is `70`; over `10 years` use `90`.

> **Key:** Hypotension in a child is not the beginning of shock. It is the last few minutes of it.

## Grading dehydration

Dehydration is graded as a percentage of body weight lost. Each kilogram lost is `1 liter` of fluid, so ask what the child weighed at the last check-up.

| | Mild, about 5% | Moderate, about 10% | Severe, 15% or more |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mental status | Normal, thirsty | Irritable or listless | Lethargic, floppy |
| Mouth | Slightly dry | Dry | Parched, no tears |
| Eyes and fontanelle | Normal | Sunken | Deeply sunken |
| Skin | Normal | Tents slowly | Tents and stays |
| Capillary refill | Under `2 s` | `2 to 3 s` | Over `3 s` |
| Heart rate | Normal | Elevated | Very high, then falling |
| Wet diapers | Slightly fewer | Fewer than `4` in `24 hours` | Almost none in `12 hours` |

A normal infant produces at least `6` wet diapers a day. "He has not had a wet diaper since last night" is a vital sign, and you should say it in your report.

## The four kinds of shock in a child

- **Hypovolemic** is the common one: vomiting and diarrhea, burns, bleeding. Dry inside, fast heart, cool skin.
- **Distributive:** sepsis or anaphylaxis. Fever, petechiae, or hives with an exposure; the skin may be warm and flushed early.
- **Cardiogenic:** myocarditis, congenital heart disease, or a rate too fast to fill. A heart rate over `220` in an infant or over `180` in a child is supraventricular tachycardia, not sinus tachycardia.
- **Obstructive:** tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, or a newborn in the first two weeks of life who suddenly turns gray as a fetal vessel closes.

## What the EMT does

Lay the child flat, keep them warm — a cold child clots poorly and burns glucose making heat — give oxygen to hold SpO2 `94%` or higher, control bleeding, and check a glucose, because low sugar travels with pediatric shock. A glucose under `60 mg/dL` in a child, or under `45 mg/dL` in a newborn, needs correcting; varies by protocol.

Fluid is an ALS intervention: `20 mL/kg` of isotonic crystalloid over `5 to 20 minutes`, reassessed and repeated to about `60 mL/kg`. Your contribution is an accurate weight, an early ALS request, and a short scene time.

> **On the exam:** Any answer choice that waits for the blood pressure to fall before acting is wrong in a pediatric shock question.
keyPoints: Children hold about 75 mL/kg of blood, so a 20 kg child's entire volume is only about 1,500 mL.
Compensation is heart rate and vasoconstriction only; tachycardia with delayed capillary refill is compensated shock.
Decompensated shock is a systolic under 70 plus twice the age in years, and it is a near-arrest finding.
Grade dehydration by mental status, mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill and wet diapers, not by blood pressure.
EMT care is position, warmth, oxygen, bleeding control, a glucose check and an early ALS request; fluid is 20 mL/kg at the ALS level.

checks.q: A 10 kg toddler with two days of vomiting and diarrhea has a heart rate of 170, capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool mottled legs, and a blood pressure of 88/54. How do you classify this?
choices: Stable, because the blood pressure is normal for age
Compensated shock, which is already severe and needs immediate transport
Decompensated shock requiring CPR
Mild dehydration
checks.why: The pressure is still above 70 plus twice the age, so he is compensating, but the heart rate, refill time and skin say he is in shock now. Waiting for the pressure to drop means waiting for arrest.

checks.q: Approximately how much total blood volume does a 20 kg five-year-old have?
choices: About 700 mL
About 1,000 mL
About 1,500 mL
About 3,000 mL
checks.why: About 75 mL/kg times 20 kg is roughly 1,500 mL. A 300 mL loss is 20 percent of his volume, which is why apparently modest bleeding is dangerous in children.

checks.q: An 8-month-old has no tears, a sunken fontanelle, skin that tents, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and two wet diapers in 24 hours. What grade of dehydration is this?
choices: Mild, about 5 percent
Moderate, about 10 percent
Severe, 15 percent or more
Cannot be graded without a blood pressure
checks.why: Tenting skin, absent tears, refill over 3 seconds and almost no urine define severe dehydration, roughly 15 percent of body weight. Blood pressure adds nothing because it falls last in children.

lessons.title: The febrile infant
lessons.body:
A fever in a `30-year-old` is a symptom. A fever in a `3-week-old` is a diagnosis in progress, and the whole system treats it that way.

## The number and the route

Fever is a rectal temperature of `100.4 F (38.0 C)` or higher. That single number drives admissions. Rectal is the standard under `3 months`; axillary and temporal readings run low, and tympanic is unreliable under `6 months`, so a reassuring forehead scan does not clear an infant.

Reported fever counts. A caregiver who says the baby felt hot and gave acetaminophen before you arrived has documented a fever, and the hospital treats it as real. Record the drug, the dose and the **time**, because the temperature you measure may be artificially normal.

> **Trap:** A fever that came down with acetaminophen proves nothing. Responding to a fever reducer does not separate a cold from bacteria in the bloodstream.

## Why infants are different

A newborn's immune system cannot wall off an infection, so organisms that would stay local in an older child spread to the blood, the urine, the lungs and the lining of the brain. The bugs are the ones picked up around birth: group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria. Herpes simplex acquired at delivery shows up at `5 to 14 days` of life with poor feeding, seizures, or a cluster of small blisters.

Because the source is invisible from the outside, age drives the plan:

| Age | What the hospital does |
|---|---|
| `0 to 28 days` | Blood, urine and spinal fluid cultures, antibiotics, admission — every time |
| `29 to 60 days` | Blood and urine, inflammatory markers, often spinal fluid; many admitted |
| `61 to 90 days` | Risk-stratified: urine and blood at minimum |
| Over `3 months`, vaccinated | Examined for a source; well-appearing children often go home |

> **Key:** An infant under `60 days` with a fever goes to the hospital even if it is smiling, feeding well and the happiest patient of your shift. "Well-appearing" is not a disposition at that age.

## The opposite sign

Very sick young infants often cannot mount a fever at all. A temperature under `96.8 F (36.0 C)` in a neonate is as ominous as `101 F`. Cold plus mottled plus feeding poorly is sepsis until proven otherwise. Warm them actively: dry clothing, blankets, a hat, and a warm compartment.

## Red flags to name out loud in your report

- Feeding under half the usual amount, or refusing the breast or bottle
- Fewer wet diapers than normal
- Grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, or pauses in breathing
- Mottled, gray or ashen skin, capillary refill over `2 seconds`
- A bulging fontanelle (pressure) or a deeply sunken one (dehydration)
- A cry nobody can console, or a baby too sleepy to wake and feed
- Petechiae, flat purple spots that do not blanch under pressure, especially below the nipple line
- A seizure, or subtle newborn twitching that looks like lip-smacking or bicycling legs

Petechiae with fever is meningococcus until it is not. Put a mask on yourself, limit who gets close, and notify the hospital early so they are not surprised at the door. Ask whether the child has had all scheduled vaccines: an unimmunized infant puts Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcus back on the list.

## What you do

Full vitals, a glucose, oxygen if saturations are low, blankets and a gentle ride. Do not cool the child with ice water, alcohol or a cold sponge — shivering raises the core temperature and burns oxygen the baby does not have. Bring the caregiver, the vaccination record if it is at hand, and the exact wording of what the family noticed first.

> **On shift:** The sentence that helps the triage nurse most is age in days, measured temperature with route, feeding, wet diapers, and what changed. "Twenty-six days old, rectal 101.2, took two ounces since midnight instead of eight, one wet diaper since 8 p.m." beats any adjective.
keyPoints: Fever in an infant is a rectal temperature of 100.4 F or 38.0 C, and rectal is the standard route under 3 months.
Any infant under 60 days with a fever goes to the hospital regardless of how well it looks.
Hypothermia under 96.8 F in a neonate is as concerning as fever and suggests sepsis.
A fever that responds to acetaminophen does not rule out serious bacterial infection; record the drug, dose and time.
Petechiae with fever means mask, minimize contact, notify early, and transport without delay.

checks.q: A 3-week-old has a rectal temperature of 100.6 F, is feeding normally, smiling and looks perfect. The parents want to wait until morning. What is correct?
choices: She needs evaluation now; every febrile infant under 28 days gets a full workup and admission
She can wait if she keeps feeding well
Give acetaminophen and recheck in an hour
She only needs to go if the fever exceeds 102 F
checks.why: Under 28 days, a rectal temperature of 100.4 F or higher means cultures of blood, urine and spinal fluid, antibiotics and admission. Appearance does not predict bacteremia at that age.

checks.q: A 5-week-old is sleepy, mottled and feeding poorly, with a rectal temperature of 96.1 F. How should you interpret the temperature?
choices: It is reassuring because there is no fever
It suggests the baby is simply cold from the room
Hypothermia in a neonate is a sepsis sign and this is a critical patient
It means a viral illness rather than bacterial
checks.why: Young infants with overwhelming infection often drop their temperature instead of raising it. Cold, mottled and poorly feeding is sepsis until proven otherwise; warm actively and transport.

lessons.title: Pediatric trauma: head, belly, and injuries that do not fit
lessons.body:
A child is not a small adult with smaller injuries. The same force lands differently because of how a child is built.

## The anatomy that decides the injury

The head is proportionally huge, about `25%` of body length at birth, so it leads in a fall and the neck absorbs the bending force. Ribs are mostly cartilage, so they bend instead of breaking: a child can have a badly bruised lung (pulmonary contusion) with a normal-looking chest and no fractures. The liver, spleen and kidneys sit lower and less covered, behind a thin abdominal wall.

> **Key:** A rib fracture in a child means the force was enormous. Rib fractures in an infant mean the force was enormous and almost always inflicted.

## Head injury

Head trauma is the leading cause of death in injured children. An infant under about `18 months` has open sutures and a fontanelle that can accommodate blood, so an infant — and only an infant — can lose enough blood inside the skull to go into shock. In an older child, hypotension after a head injury means bleeding somewhere else. Go find it.

Your entire job is preventing the second injury. Keep SpO2 at `94%` or higher, keep the systolic pressure above the floor for age, keep them warm, and do **not** hyperventilate. Ventilate an apneic child at `1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds`. Faster than that drives carbon dioxide down, narrows brain vessels, and starves the injured brain.

Watch for the late signs. A rising blood pressure with a falling heart rate and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad) means rising pressure inside the skull and is a preterminal finding. Vomiting once after a head strike is common; three or more episodes, a worsening headache, a child who is not acting like themselves, any seizure, or a bulging fontanelle changes everything.

## The abdomen

Children hold a normal blood pressure while bleeding into the belly, so a distended, tender, guarded abdomen may be your only clue. Two patterns are worth memorizing:

- **Handlebar injury:** a bicycle handlebar to the upper abdomen bruises the duodenum or pancreas. A small bruise, pain out of proportion, vomiting — and the real injury declares itself hours later.
- **Seatbelt sign:** a horizontal bruise across the lower abdomen from a lap belt means hollow organ injury and a possible spine fracture behind it. It goes to a pediatric trauma center.

Crying children swallow air and bag-valve-mask ventilation inflates the stomach. A distended stomach pushes the diaphragm up, mimics abdominal injury and makes ventilation worse. Note it; do not try to fix it in the field.

One more: **commotio cordis**, a baseball, puck or fist striking the chest at exactly the wrong `20 milliseconds` of the cardiac cycle, throws a structurally normal heart into ventricular fibrillation. The treatment is immediate CPR and the AED, and nothing else.

## Spine and packaging

Children can have a spinal cord injury with normal imaging (SCIWORA) because their ligaments stretch further than the cord does. Treat the mechanism, not the film.

When you immobilize, respect the occiput. Lying flat on a board flexes a small child's neck and closes the airway. Pad from the shoulders to the hips until the ear canal lines up with the shoulder.

## When the story does not fit

Physical abuse hides inside ordinary complaints. The most usable field screen is bruising:

- **TEN-4:** bruising on the **torso**, **ear** or **neck** in a child `4` years old or younger, or **any** bruise on an infant under `4 months`.
- **FACES-P:** bruising of the **frenulum**, **angle of the jaw**, **cheek**, **eyelid** or **sclera**, or any **patterned** bruise.

A torn frenulum in a baby, burns with clean waterline edges, a spiral fracture in a child who does not yet walk, a delay in seeking care, and a story that changes between tellings all belong in your report — in the caregiver's own words, in quotation marks. Infants who cannot roll over do not fall off couches.

> **On shift:** You document; you do not investigate or confront. Record what you saw, what you were told, who was present, and the position the child was found in. In New Jersey every person is a mandated reporter, and the emergency department must hear your concern before you leave.
keyPoints: Flexible ribs mean a child can have a severe lung contusion with no fractures; rib fractures signal massive or inflicted force.
Only infants with open fontanelles can bleed enough inside the skull to cause shock; in older children hypotension means bleeding elsewhere.
Prevent the second injury: SpO2 94 percent or higher, adequate pressure, warmth, and 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds with no hyperventilation.
Handlebar injuries and seatbelt signs predict deep injury that shows up hours later, so both go to a pediatric trauma center.
TEN-4-FACES-P bruising, injuries impossible for the child's stage, delayed care and changing stories are the abuse screen; document quotes, do not investigate.

checks.q: A 9-month-old is brought in after 'rolling off the couch.' He has bruising on his left ear and a torn frenulum inside his upper lip. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Normal findings for a mobile infant
Inflicted injury, since ear bruising and a torn frenulum are high-specificity abuse findings
A bleeding disorder is the most likely cause
Nothing, because the story explains it
checks.why: TEN-4-FACES-P flags ear bruising in a child 4 or under and frenulum injury at any age. Babies do not bruise their ears on furniture. Document the quotes and report.

checks.q: A 5-year-old struck by a car is apneic with a head injury. What ventilation rate is correct?
choices: 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds
1 breath every second, to drive carbon dioxide down
1 breath every 6 seconds
As fast as the bag allows until the pupils change
checks.why: Routine hyperventilation constricts cerebral vessels and worsens the injury. Ventilate at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, keep saturations at or above 94 percent, and keep the pressure up.

checks.q: Why do you pad from the shoulders to the hips when immobilizing a 2-year-old?
choices: For comfort on a long transport
To raise the chest for easier compressions
Because the large occiput flexes the neck when the child lies flat, which closes the airway
To keep the straps from loosening
checks.why: A small child's head is proportionally large, so lying flat pushes the neck into flexion. Padding the torso restores neutral alignment, with the ear canal level with the shoulder.

lessons.title: Children with special healthcare needs: when the device fails
lessons.body:
The parent of a child with a tracheostomy has managed that airway `10,000` times. You have not. So the first move on every one of these calls is one question: "What do you normally do when this happens?"

The second thing to establish is baseline. A child with chronic lung disease may live at `88%` on room air, and a child with a neurologic injury may sit at a heart rate of `120` all day. Ask what normal is before you decide what abnormal means.

## Case 1: the trach that stops working

A `4-year-old` with a tracheostomy is in distress and dusky. Work through **DOPE**:

- **D**isplacement — has the tube come out or shifted? Look at the flange and the ties.
- **O**bstruction — is it plugged with mucus? Suction it.
- **P**neumothorax — sudden distress with one-sided chest movement.
- **E**quipment — circuit disconnected, battery dead, oxygen tank empty.

If the tube is in place, suction first. Catheter size in French is roughly twice the tube size: a `4.0` tube takes an `8 Fr` catheter. Insert only to the premeasured depth the family uses, apply suction **on the way out** for no more than `5 to 10 seconds`, and give oxygen before and after. Suction pressure is about `60 to 100 mmHg` for infants and `100 to 120 mmHg` for children — varies by protocol.

If the tube is out and the family has a spare, they will usually replace it faster than you can. If it cannot be replaced, ventilate anyway: seal an infant mask over the **stoma** and bag there, or if the upper airway is open, cover the stoma with a gloved hand and bag the mouth and nose normally.

> **Key:** A trach in distress is a plugged trach until proven otherwise. Suction, then ventilate. Do not stand there troubleshooting a machine while a child turns blue.

## Case 2: the home ventilator

Disconnect the vent and bag the patient. That one move solves most ventilator calls and converts a machine problem into a problem you understand. A high-pressure alarm means obstruction: secretions, a kink, or the child biting the tube. A low-pressure alarm means a leak or a disconnection. Bring the machine, the circuit, the battery and the written settings: mode, rate, tidal volume, pressure, PEEP and oxygen percentage.

## Case 3: the VP shunt

A ventriculoperitoneal shunt drains cerebrospinal fluid from the brain to the abdomen. When it blocks, pressure rises: headache, repeated vomiting, sleepiness, irritability, a bulging fontanelle in an infant, and eyes that drift downward, called sunsetting. When it is infected, add fever, redness or swelling along the tubing under the skin, and abdominal pain.

Elevate the head about `30 degrees` if there is no spinal concern, hold SpO2 at `94%` or higher, do not press or pump the valve behind the ear, and transport to the hospital that placed it when that is reasonable. A blocked shunt is time-critical.

## Case 4: the feeding tube

Gastrostomy tubes come out. The tract can start to close within `hours`, so bring the tube with you, cover the site with a dry dressing, and note the time it came out. Do not reinsert one unless your protocol and training allow it, and never put medication or fluid into a tube you have not confirmed is in place.

Missed feeds matter. Many of these children have almost no glucose reserve, so check a blood sugar on any tube-fed child who is acting differently.

## The rest of the go-bag

Ports and central lines: do not access them, keep the site clean, and clamp a line that is open to air. Vagus nerve stimulators for seizures often come with a magnet the family swipes across the chest. A baclofen pump that fails causes fever, rigidity and altered mental status, and that is a true emergency. Whatever the device, transport the caregiver, the equipment and the binder they hand you at the door.

> **On shift:** Address the child, not the caregiver, even when the child cannot answer. Then ask the caregiver the two questions that run the call: what is normal for him, and what do you do at home when this happens?
keyPoints: Establish the child's baseline first: many live at saturations or heart rates that would alarm you in a healthy child.
Run DOPE for any trach or ventilator emergency: displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment.
Suction a trach on the way out for 5 to 10 seconds; catheter French size is about twice the tube size.
If a vent is alarming and the child is in distress, disconnect it and bag through the trach.
Shunt malfunction is headache, vomiting, lethargy, irritability and sunsetting eyes; elevate the head, never pump the valve, transport.

checks.q: A ventilator-dependent 6-year-old is in distress and the machine is alarming with a high-pressure alert. What is your first action?
choices: Adjust the ventilator settings to lower the pressure
Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate with a bag-valve mask through the trach, then suction
Wait for the caregiver to reset the alarm
Remove the tracheostomy tube
checks.why: Take the machine out of the equation and ventilate manually. A high-pressure alarm usually means secretions or a kink, so suctioning comes next. Never adjust settings you do not manage.

checks.q: A gastrostomy tube fell out 45 minutes ago and the site is leaking. What do you do?
choices: Reinsert it immediately so the tract stays open
Flush the stoma with saline
Cover the site with a dry dressing, bring the tube, note the time it came out, and transport
Nothing is needed; it can wait for the next clinic visit
checks.why: The tract can close within hours, which is why the time out matters and the hospital needs to know it. Reinsertion is not an EMT skill unless a protocol specifically allows it.

lessons.title: After the baby: hemorrhage, rupture and preterm labor
lessons.body:
The deliveries that go wrong after the baby is out kill faster than the ones that go wrong during. Obstetric hemorrhage is a leading cause of maternal death, and most of it yields to pressure, warmth and speed.

## The four causes of postpartum bleeding

Hemorrhage is more than `500 mL` after a vaginal birth, or any bleeding that makes her unstable. Memorize the **four Ts**:

1. **Tone** — the uterus fails to clamp down (atony). `70 to 80%` of cases.
2. **Trauma** — a tear of the perineum, vagina or cervix. Steady bright bleeding with a firm uterus.
3. **Tissue** — a fragment of placenta left behind keeps the uterus from closing.
4. **Thrombin** — a clotting problem, including the one you cause by letting her get cold.

Risk rises with a long labor, a large baby, twins, many prior deliveries, and a very fast delivery.

## What you do, in order

1. **Massage the fundus.** One hand cups the top of the uterus below the navel and kneads firmly until it feels like a grapefruit. The other hand presses just above the pubic bone to support the lower uterus so you do not invert it.
2. **Put the baby to the breast.** Nursing releases oxytocin, the body's own drug for exactly this, within minutes.
3. **Empty the bladder.** A full bladder physically blocks the uterus from contracting. If she can void, let her.
4. **Pressure on what you can see.** A perineal tear gets direct pressure with gauze. Nothing goes inside the vagina — no packing, ever.
5. **Count.** A fully soaked perineal pad holds roughly `100 mL`; a saturated underpad holds far more. Report a count and a clock time, not "a lot."
6. **Treat the shock.** Supine with legs elevated, high-flow oxygen, aggressive warming, ALS intercept, and an early radio call so blood is waiting.

> **Trap:** Never pull the cord to speed the placenta. Traction can turn the uterus inside out. Uterine inversion looks like a dark red mass at the opening with shock far out of proportion to visible blood: do not remove the placenta, cover with moist dressings, treat shock, and go.

## Uterine rupture

The uterus tears open, usually along an old cesarean scar, or after blunt trauma. The story is distinctive: strong labor, a sudden sharp tearing pain, and then the **contractions stop**. The abdomen becomes tender and irregularly shaped, fetal parts may be easy to feel through the wall, and she slides into shock with little external bleeding. This is an operating-room emergency measured in minutes: oxygen, left tilt, shock care, fastest reasonable transport, early notification.

## Amniotic fluid embolism

Rare, roughly `1 in 40,000` deliveries, and worth recognizing because it resembles nothing else. During labor or within `30 minutes` of delivery she suddenly cannot breathe, her pressure collapses, she may seize, and then she bleeds from everywhere including old puncture sites because her clotting has failed. There is no field treatment beyond airway, oxygen, ventilation, CPR if she arrests, left uterine displacement and immediate transport. Recognize it, say it on the radio, and drive.

## Preterm labor

Regular contractions before `37 weeks`. The symptoms are vaguer than term labor: rhythmic tightening, a constant low backache, pelvic pressure, a change in discharge, or a leak of fluid. If the membranes ruptured, note the **time** and the **color** of the fluid.

Field care: left lateral position, oxygen if saturations are low, nothing in the vagina, keep her calm and warm, do not encourage pushing, and choose a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit if one is within reasonable reach. For preterm labor, the transport decision is the treatment. Give gestational age and contraction timing on the radio.

If delivery happens anyway, split the crew: one person owns the mother, one owns the baby. Preheat the compartment to about `78 F (26 C)` before the birth, because cold is the newborn's biggest enemy for the next `10 minutes`.

> **On the exam:** For preterm labor in the field the answer is almost always position, oxygen, no vaginal exam, and transport to a hospital that can care for a premature newborn.
keyPoints: Postpartum hemorrhage is over 500 mL or any bleeding causing instability; the four Ts are tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin, and tone causes 70 to 80 percent.
EMT sequence: two-handed fundal massage, baby to the breast, empty the bladder, direct pressure on visible tears, count pads, treat shock and keep her warm.
Cord traction can invert the uterus; never pull, and never pack the vagina.
Uterine rupture is sudden tearing pain with contractions that stop, shock, and little external bleeding.
Preterm labor care is left lateral, nothing per vagina, no pushing, and transport to a hospital with a NICU with early notification.

checks.q: Two minutes of fundal massage has not firmed the uterus and she is still bleeding. Which next step is within EMT scope?
choices: Put the newborn to the breast and have her empty her bladder, while continuing massage
Pack the vagina with sterile gauze
Apply gentle traction on the cord to remove any retained placenta
Administer oxytocin intramuscularly
checks.why: Nursing releases the mother's own oxytocin and a full bladder physically prevents the uterus from contracting. Packing is never done, cord traction risks inversion, and oxytocin is not an EMT medication.

checks.q: A patient with a prior cesarean is in strong labor when she has sudden severe tearing abdominal pain and her contractions stop. She is now pale with a heart rate of 130 and minimal vaginal bleeding. What is happening?
choices: Placenta previa
Uterine rupture with concealed internal bleeding
Normal transition in labor
Amniotic fluid embolism
checks.why: Prior cesarean scar, tearing pain, contractions ceasing and shock with little visible blood is uterine rupture. Previa bleeds brightly and painlessly; amniotic fluid embolism begins with sudden hypoxia and collapse.

checks.q: You are transporting a patient in preterm labor at 31 weeks with no crowning. What is the single most important decision?
choices: Whether to perform a vaginal exam to check dilation
Whether to encourage her to push and deliver in the truck
Which hospital you transport to, ideally one with a newborn intensive care unit
Whether to give her oxygen at 15 L/min regardless of saturations
checks.why: Destination is the treatment for preterm labor, because a premature newborn needs a NICU. Vaginal exams are never done by EMTs, pushing is discouraged, and oxygen is titrated to saturation.

lessons.title: Neonatal resuscitation minute by minute
lessons.body:
You already know the steps. This is the clock that holds them together. Run it out loud, because saying the time is what keeps a two-person crew synchronized.

## Before the baby comes

Ask four questions: how many weeks, how many babies, was the fluid clear, and are there any known problems. Then set up: warm the compartment to about `78 F (26 C)`, open two dry towels and a hat, lay out an infant bag-valve mask (a `240 mL` bag) with size `0` and size `1` masks, a bulb syringe, two clamps, and start a clock.

## The script

**0:00 — Birth.** Say the time out loud and start the timer. Ask three questions in about `5 seconds`: term, good tone, breathing or crying?

Three yes answers: dry, place skin to skin on the mother, hat on, monitor. Stop there.

**0:00 to 0:30 — Initial steps.** Warm, dry vigorously, remove the wet towel, stimulate by rubbing the back and flicking the soles, position the head neutral to slightly extended with a small roll under the shoulders, and clear the mouth then the nose only if secretions obstruct.

**0:30 — First decision point.** Look at breathing and check the heart rate at the base of the cord, or listen over the chest for `6 seconds` and multiply by `10`.

- Apneic, gasping, **or** heart rate under `100`: start positive-pressure ventilation now at `40 to 60 breaths per minute`. Say "breathe, two, three" out loud to hold the rate. Start with room air for a term baby, `21 to 30%` oxygen for a preterm baby if you can blend.
- Breathing with a heart rate over `100` but labored or centrally blue: keep warm, consider blow-by oxygen or CPAP per protocol, reassess.

**0:45 — If the chest is not rising, fix that before anything else.** Run **MR SOPA** in order: **M**ask adjust, **R**eposition the head, **S**uction mouth and nose, **O**pen the mouth slightly, **P**ressure increase gradually, **A**irway alternative. Ventilation that does not move the chest is not ventilation.

**1:00 — Score the first APGAR and reassess.** A rising heart rate is the single best sign your ventilation is working.

**1:00 to 1:30 — Second decision point,** after `30 seconds` of ventilation that visibly moves the chest:

- Heart rate over `100` and breathing on its own: stop ventilating, keep warm, monitor.
- Heart rate `60 to 99`: keep ventilating and recheck the seal and the head position.
- Heart rate under `60`: add **compressions** at `3` compressions to `1` breath, `120 events per minute` (`90` compressions and `30` breaths each minute), two-thumb encircling technique, depth one third of the chest, and increase oxygen to `100%`.

Reassess after `60 seconds` of coordinated compressions and ventilation; some EMT protocols still say `30 seconds`, so follow yours. Stop compressions once the rate is over `60`. Stop ventilating once it is over `100` with spontaneous breathing. Epinephrine `0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg` is an ALS drug for a rate that stays under `60`; your contribution is getting that unit moving early.

## Oxygen targets by the minute

Do not chase `100%`. A healthy newborn takes `10 minutes` to pink up. Measure on the **right hand**.

| Minutes of life | Target SpO2 |
|---|---|
| 1 | `60 to 65%` |
| 2 | `65 to 70%` |
| 3 | `70 to 75%` |
| 4 | `75 to 80%` |
| 5 | `80 to 85%` |
| 10 | `85 to 95%` |

> **Trap:** A baby at `3 minutes` with a saturation of `72%`, a heart rate of `150` and a strong cry is normal. Treating that number is how newborns end up over-oxygenated.

## The premature newborn

Under `32 weeks`, do **not** dry the body. Slide the baby straight into a food-grade plastic bag or wrap in plastic to the neck, dry only the head, and put a hat on. Target a temperature of `36.5 to 37.5 C`. Thermal care is resuscitation for these babies.

> **Key:** Where it goes wrong is almost always mechanical: a mask leak, a flexed or over-extended neck, bagging too fast, starting compressions before `30 seconds` of effective ventilation, a cold compartment, and no hat. Five of those six are free to fix.
keyPoints: Say the time of birth out loud and start a clock; the newborn algorithm is a 30-second cycle.
Start PPV at 40 to 60 per minute for apnea, gasping or a heart rate under 100, using room air in a term baby.
If the chest does not rise, run MR SOPA before adding anything else.
Compressions start only after 30 seconds of chest-rising ventilation with a heart rate under 60: 3 to 1, 120 events per minute, two thumbs.
Preductal SpO2 targets climb by the minute, reaching only 80 to 85 percent at 5 minutes; under 32 weeks, wrap in plastic without drying the body.

checks.q: You have been giving positive-pressure ventilation to a newborn for 30 seconds but the chest is not rising. The heart rate is 70. What do you do next?
choices: Begin chest compressions at 3 to 1
Increase the rate to 100 breaths per minute
Run MR SOPA: mask, reposition, suction, open the mouth, increase pressure, alternative airway
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen
checks.why: Compressions are useless without effective ventilation. MR SOPA fixes the mechanical causes of a non-rising chest. Only after the chest rises for 30 seconds and the rate is still under 60 do you compress.

checks.q: A term newborn is 3 minutes old, crying strongly, heart rate 150, with a preductal SpO2 of 72%. What is the correct action?
choices: This is within the normal target range for 3 minutes of life; keep warm and monitor
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Begin positive-pressure ventilation
Begin compressions
checks.why: Targets at 3 minutes are 70 to 75 percent. A vigorous baby with a good heart rate is transitioning normally, and pushing high-concentration oxygen into a healthy newborn does harm rather than good.

checks.q: A baby is delivered at 29 weeks. What is the correct thermal management?
choices: Dry vigorously, then wrap in two warm blankets
Place in a food-grade plastic bag or plastic wrap without drying the body, dry the head, add a hat
Apply chemical heat packs directly to the skin
Keep the compartment at normal room temperature to avoid overheating
checks.why: Under 32 weeks, plastic wrap applied without drying traps evaporative heat far better than towels. Heat packs go over a blanket layer only, and hypothermia sharply increases mortality in premature newborns.

lessons.title: Geriatric syndromes: the fall workup, delirium and the pill bottle
lessons.body:
Older patients rarely arrive with one disease. They arrive with a syndrome — a fall, confusion, weakness — that has four causes stacked on top of each other, and the pill bottles usually explain two of them.

## A fall is a workup, not a diagnosis

One in four adults over `65` falls each year, and falls are the leading cause of injury death in that group. The question is never whether she fell. It is why.

Ask, in this order:

1. What were you doing at the moment it happened?
2. Do you remember hitting the ground? A gap means syncope, not a trip.
3. Anything right before it — chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, the room spinning, one-sided weakness?
4. Any new medication or dose change in the last `2 weeks`?
5. How long were you on the floor?

That last answer changes the call. A **long lie** over `1 hour` adds hypothermia, dehydration, pressure injury to skin and muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) that can shut down the kidneys. Dark, tea-colored urine after a long lie is worth saying out loud at the door.

> **Key:** Syncope and a mechanical trip look identical on arrival and mean completely different things. If she cannot tell you how she reached the floor, treat it as a cardiac or neurologic event until the hospital says otherwise.

Check for a hip fracture: groin pain, the leg shortened and rotated outward, inability to bear weight. Some patients with a hip fracture still walk, so groin or hip pain after any fall goes in.

Then look at the room and put it in your report: throw rugs, no grab bars, a walker parked across the room, dim lighting, stairs full of clutter, an empty refrigerator, a week of pills poured into one dish.

## Orthostatic numbers

A fall of `20 mmHg` systolic or `10 mmHg` diastolic within `3 minutes` of standing, or a heart rate rise over `20`, is orthostatic hypotension. It is the mechanism behind a large share of falls, and the cause is usually a drug.

## Delirium versus dementia, second pass

Delirium is acute brain failure caused by something outside the brain. The version everyone misses is the **quiet** one: a patient who is withdrawn, slow and sleepy gets labeled as "just her dementia" or as depression, and goes home with an untreated urinary infection and a low sodium.

Ask the family the only question that separates them: **is this how she was two days ago?** Then hunt causes: infection, low oxygen, new or stopped medications including alcohol, glucose, sodium, pain, constipation or a full bladder, and stroke.

Document a baseline the hospital can use. "Daughter states patient normally does the crossword and cooks dinner; today she does not know her daughter's name" is worth more than the word confused.

## Three pill-bottle cases

**Case 1.** An `80-year-old` on lisinopril starts tamsulosin for bladder symptoms, stands up at night, and falls. Both drugs lower standing blood pressure. The fall is a drug effect, and it repeats tomorrow night if nobody names it.

**Case 2.** A `76-year-old` on apixaban struck his head two days ago and is slower than usual today. Anticoagulants turn a minor head strike into a slow subdural bleed that declares itself days later. He goes in regardless of the exam.

**Case 3.** An `82-year-old` on glipizide skipped lunch. Glucose `38 mg/dL`, fully awake after oral glucose, and she wants to stay home. Sulfonylureas keep working for `12 to 24 hours`, so the hypoglycemia comes back once the sugar is used up. This is a transport, not a refusal.

Two more worth knowing cold: **digoxin** toxicity (nausea, yellow-green halos around lights, a slow or irregular pulse) and **anticholinergics** such as diphenhydramine or oxybutynin, which cause confusion, urinary retention and falls in older adults.

## Elder abuse patterns

Financial exploitation is the most common form. Neglect is the most visible: pressure ulcers, weight loss, dirty clothing, prescriptions unfilled for weeks. Physical signs include bruising on the inner arms, wrists or neck, and injuries in several stages of healing.

The behavioral pattern matters more than any single bruise: a caregiver who will not leave the room, who answers questions asked of the patient, and a patient who looks at the caregiver before speaking. Try to get `60 seconds` alone during the move to the stretcher.

> **On shift:** Report facts and direct quotes, never conclusions. Reports go to your county Adult Protective Services office, and for a patient in a nursing home or assisted living the state Office of the Ombudsman for the Institutionalized Elderly takes it. Tell the emergency department nurse before you leave the building.
keyPoints: A fall is a symptom: establish whether she remembers hitting the ground, what preceded it, new medications in 2 weeks, and how long she was down.
A long lie over 1 hour risks hypothermia, dehydration, pressure injury and rhabdomyolysis.
Orthostatic hypotension is a 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic drop within 3 minutes of standing, usually caused by a drug.
Quiet, hypoactive delirium is the version that gets missed; the decisive question is whether this is her baseline two days ago.
Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 12 to 24 hours, so a patient who wakes up with oral glucose still requires transport.

checks.q: An 84-year-old was found on her bathroom floor and thinks she was there since about 10 p.m., roughly 8 hours. What complications should you anticipate?
choices: None beyond the obvious bruising
Hypothermia, dehydration, pressure injury and muscle breakdown affecting the kidneys
Only a hip fracture
Only psychological distress
checks.why: A long lie over an hour causes progressive heat loss, fluid loss, skin breakdown over bony points and rhabdomyolysis. Tea-colored urine is a late clue and belongs in your report.

checks.q: An 82-year-old on glipizide had a glucose of 38 mg/dL, is fully alert after oral glucose, and refuses transport. What is the concern?
choices: None; she is corrected and can refuse
Sulfonylureas keep lowering glucose for 12 to 24 hours, so the hypoglycemia will recur
Oral glucose causes rebound hyperglycemia
She needs a second dose of oral glucose and can then stay
checks.why: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea that pushes the pancreas to release insulin for many hours. The sugar you gave is consumed and the patient drops again, often unobserved. Encourage transport strongly and document the refusal.

checks.q: A daughter says her mother 'has dementia and gets confused.' The patient has been sleepy and withdrawn since yesterday. What do you do with that information?
choices: Accept dementia as the explanation and transport routinely
Ask whether this is how she was two days ago, and if not, treat it as delirium and hunt for a cause
Perform a stroke scale and, if it is negative, leave her at home
Document confusion and move on
checks.why: Dementia is slow and steady; a change over hours to days is delirium, which is a medical emergency with an external cause such as infection, hypoxia, medications or glucose. The baseline question separates them.

cards.front: What three problems happen at once in an asthma attack?
cards.back: Bronchospasm, swelling of the airway lining, and thick mucus plugging. Albuterol relaxes only the muscle, which is why a child may still work hard after a good treatment.

cards.front: How do you grade an asthma attack by what the child can say?
cards.back: Full sentences is mild, short phrases is moderate, single words is severe. A drowsy child who has stopped talking, with a quiet chest, is in respiratory failure.

cards.front: Why is a quiet chest in a struggling asthmatic an emergency?
cards.back: No air is moving, so nothing can wheeze. It signals impending respiratory arrest. Assist ventilations slowly and call ALS; do not read it as improvement.

cards.front: What are the nebulized and inhaler doses of albuterol for a child?
cards.back: Nebulized 2.5 mg in 3 mL at 6 to 8 L/min, or 1.25 mg in the youngest children in some systems. By inhaler, 90 mcg per puff, usually 2 puffs with a spacer. Varies by protocol.

cards.front: How do you tell bronchiolitis from asthma at the bedside?
cards.back: Bronchiolitis: under 2, first or second episode, days of runny nose first, wet crackles with the wheeze, little response to albuterol. Asthma: over 2, repeat attacks, known triggers, dry wheeze that improves.

cards.front: What is the highest-yield intervention for an infant with bronchiolitis?
cards.back: Suction the nose. Infants under about 4 months depend on nasal breathing, so clearing the nose can transform the work of breathing. Then oxygen and head elevation.

cards.front: Why do you ventilate a wheezing child slowly with full exhalation?
cards.back: Obstructed airways empty slowly. Stacking breaths traps air, raises pressure in the chest, reduces venous return, and drops the blood pressure.

cards.front: What does stridor tell you about the location of an obstruction?
cards.back: Stridor is a harsh crowing sound on inhalation and means narrowing at or just below the vocal cords. Snoring is the tongue; wheezing on exhalation is deep in the chest.

cards.front: What is bacterial tracheitis and how does it announce itself?
cards.back: A bacterial infection layering pus in the trachea, usually after croup. Days of barky cough, then hours of high fever, a toxic-looking child, and worsening stridor that does not respond to nebulized epinephrine.

cards.front: How do you grade croup severity in the field?
cards.back: Mild: barky cough, stridor only when upset. Moderate: stridor at rest with retractions, still interactive. Severe: stridor at rest, deep retractions, agitation or lethargy, pale or dusky.

cards.front: What does the hospital give for moderate to severe croup?
cards.back: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and nebulized epinephrine for stridor at rest. Some EMS systems carry nebulized epinephrine; it varies by protocol.

cards.front: A choking child is coughing forcefully and crying. What do you do?
cards.back: Nothing but encourage coughing. Good air exchange means a partial obstruction; back blows or thrusts can turn it complete. Position of comfort, oxygen if tolerated, transport, and watch for sudden silence.

cards.front: How do you relieve a complete airway obstruction in an infant under 1 year?
cards.back: Five back slaps between the shoulder blades with the head lower than the body, then five chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower half of the sternum. Repeat. No abdominal thrusts.

cards.front: What changes when a choking child becomes unresponsive?
cards.back: Start CPR beginning with compressions, which generate more airway pressure than back slaps. Look in the mouth before each rescue breath and remove the object only if you can see it. Never sweep blindly.

cards.front: Why is a button battery an emergency even if breathing is normal?
cards.back: A lodged button battery burns through esophageal tissue in as little as 2 hours. It is a time-critical transport regardless of how well the child appears.

cards.front: How much blood does a child have per kilogram?
cards.back: About 75 mL/kg; an infant closer to 80 mL/kg and an adult about 70 mL/kg. A 20 kg five-year-old has roughly 1,500 mL total.

cards.front: Why is tachycardia a child's whole compensation strategy in shock?
cards.back: Cardiac output is rate times stroke volume, and a young heart cannot meaningfully increase stroke volume. So the only options are beating faster and vasoconstricting, which is why skin signs appear first.

cards.front: What separates compensated from decompensated shock in a child?
cards.back: Compensated: tachycardia, cool mottled skin, refill over 2 seconds, normal blood pressure. Decompensated: systolic below 70 plus twice the age in years, weak central pulse, and a child who has gone quiet.

cards.front: How is dehydration graded by percentage of body weight?
cards.back: About 5 percent is mild, about 10 percent moderate, 15 percent or more severe. Each kilogram lost equals 1 liter of fluid, so a pre-illness weight is useful history.

cards.front: How many wet diapers a day is normal for an infant, and what is concerning?
cards.back: At least 6 a day is normal. Fewer than 4 in 24 hours suggests moderate dehydration, and almost none in 12 hours suggests severe dehydration.

cards.front: Name the four categories of shock in children with one cause each.
cards.back: Hypovolemic (vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding), distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis), cardiogenic (myocarditis, SVT), obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, a closing fetal vessel in a newborn).

cards.front: What heart rate suggests SVT rather than sinus tachycardia in a child?
cards.back: Over 220 in an infant or over 180 in a child, usually without beat-to-beat variation and without a history that explains it. It is an ALS problem.

cards.front: What is the ALS fluid bolus for a child in shock, and what is the EMT's job?
cards.back: 20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid over 5 to 20 minutes, reassessed and repeated to about 60 mL/kg. The EMT supplies an accurate weight, warmth, oxygen, glucose check, early ALS and short scene time.

cards.front: What temperature defines fever in an infant, and by what route?
cards.back: 100.4 F or 38.0 C rectally. Rectal is the standard under 3 months; temporal and axillary run low and tympanic is unreliable under 6 months.

cards.front: What does the hospital do for a febrile infant aged 0 to 28 days?
cards.back: Blood, urine and spinal fluid cultures, antibiotics, and admission, every time. Appearance does not change the plan at that age.

cards.front: Does a fever that came down with acetaminophen change the plan?
cards.back: No. Response to a fever reducer does not distinguish a virus from bacteria in the blood. Record the drug, dose and time, because your measured temperature may be falsely normal.

cards.front: Why is hypothermia in a neonate as concerning as fever?
cards.back: Overwhelmed young infants often cannot mount a fever and drop their temperature instead. Under 96.8 F or 36.0 C, with mottling and poor feeding, treat it as sepsis and warm actively.

cards.front: List five red flags in a febrile infant.
cards.back: Feeding under half the usual amount, fewer wet diapers, grunting or apnea, mottled or gray skin with refill over 2 seconds, a bulging fontanelle, inconsolable crying or being unrousable, and non-blanching petechiae.

cards.front: Which organisms cause serious infection in the first month of life?
cards.back: Group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria from around the time of birth. Herpes simplex appears at 5 to 14 days with poor feeding, seizures or small blisters.

cards.front: Why should you never cool a febrile child with ice water or alcohol?
cards.back: It causes shivering, which raises core temperature and burns oxygen and glucose. Remove excess clothing instead and let the hospital give an antipyretic.

cards.front: Why can a child have a severe lung injury with a normal-looking chest?
cards.back: Pediatric ribs are largely cartilage, so force transmits through them without breaking them. Pulmonary contusion is common without any fracture; a fractured rib means enormous force.

cards.front: Which patients can bleed into the skull enough to cause shock?
cards.back: Only infants with open fontanelles and sutures, under roughly 18 months. In any older child, hypotension after head injury means bleeding somewhere else, so keep looking.

cards.front: How do you prevent secondary brain injury in a child?
cards.back: Keep SpO2 at 94 percent or higher, keep systolic pressure above the floor for age, keep them warm, and ventilate at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds without hyperventilating.

cards.front: What is Cushing's triad and what does it mean in a child?
cards.back: Rising blood pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing. It signals dangerously high pressure inside the skull and is a preterminal finding requiring immediate transport.

cards.front: What do a handlebar injury and a seatbelt sign predict?
cards.back: Handlebar to the upper abdomen injures the duodenum or pancreas and declares itself hours later. A horizontal lap-belt bruise means hollow organ injury and possible lumbar spine fracture. Both go to a pediatric trauma center.

cards.front: What is commotio cordis and how is it treated?
cards.back: A blow to the chest at exactly the wrong moment in the cardiac cycle throws a normal heart into ventricular fibrillation. Treatment is immediate CPR and the AED, nothing else.

cards.front: What is SCIWORA and how does it change your packaging?
cards.back: Spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality: a child's ligaments stretch more than the cord does. Treat the mechanism, and pad from shoulders to hips so the large occiput does not flex the neck.

cards.front: What does TEN-4-FACES-P screen for?
cards.back: Bruising that suggests abuse: torso, ear or neck bruising in a child 4 or under, any bruise on an infant under 4 months, or bruising of the frenulum, jaw angle, cheek, eyelid, sclera, or any patterned bruise.

cards.front: What are the two questions that run a special-needs call?
cards.back: What is normal for this child, and what do you do at home when this happens? Baseline saturations and heart rates are often abnormal, and the caregiver has managed the device thousands of times.

cards.front: What does DOPE stand for in a trach or ventilator emergency?
cards.back: Displacement of the tube, Obstruction with secretions, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Work through it in order, and ventilate manually while you do.

cards.front: How do you suction a tracheostomy tube correctly?
cards.back: Catheter French size is about twice the tube size, so a 4.0 tube takes an 8 Fr catheter. Insert to the family's premeasured depth, suction only on the way out for 5 to 10 seconds, and oxygenate before and after.

cards.front: The trach tube is out and cannot be replaced. How do you ventilate?
cards.back: Seal an infant mask over the stoma and bag there, or if the upper airway is patent, cover the stoma with a gloved hand and bag the mouth and nose normally.

cards.front: What do high-pressure and low-pressure ventilator alarms mean?
cards.back: High pressure means obstruction: secretions, a kink, or biting. Low pressure means a leak or disconnection. Either way, disconnect the vent and bag the patient first.

cards.front: How does a blocked VP shunt present, and what do you do?
cards.back: Headache, repeated vomiting, sleepiness, irritability, bulging fontanelle in an infant, and downward drifting eyes. Elevate the head about 30 degrees, keep SpO2 at 94 percent or higher, never pump the valve, transport promptly.

cards.front: A gastrostomy tube has fallen out. What matters most?
cards.back: The tract can begin closing within hours. Note the time it came out, cover the site with a dry dressing, bring the tube, and do not reinsert unless protocol and training allow. Check a glucose if feeds were missed.

cards.front: What are the four Ts of postpartum hemorrhage?
cards.back: Tone (uterine atony, 70 to 80 percent of cases), Trauma (perineal, vaginal or cervical tears), Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (clotting failure, worsened by hypothermia).

cards.front: How do you perform two-handed fundal massage?
cards.back: One hand cups the fundus below the navel and kneads firmly until it feels like a grapefruit; the other presses just above the pubic bone to support the lower uterus so it cannot invert.

cards.front: Besides massage, what two free interventions help a bleeding postpartum uterus?
cards.back: Put the newborn to the breast, because nursing releases the mother's own oxytocin, and empty the bladder, because a full bladder physically blocks the uterus from contracting.

cards.front: How do you quantify postpartum blood loss in your report?
cards.back: Count pads and give a time. A fully soaked perineal pad holds roughly 100 mL and a saturated underpad far more. Report a number and an interval instead of 'a lot'.

cards.front: What is uterine inversion and what causes it?
cards.back: The uterus turned inside out, usually by traction on the cord. A dark mass appears at the opening with shock out of proportion to visible blood. Do not remove the placenta, cover with moist dressings, treat shock, transport.

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of uterine rupture?
cards.back: Strong labor, then sudden tearing abdominal pain, and contractions stop. Tender irregular abdomen, easily palpable fetal parts, and shock with minimal external bleeding. Surgical emergency.

cards.front: What does amniotic fluid embolism look like?
cards.back: During labor or within 30 minutes of delivery: sudden severe breathlessness, collapse of blood pressure, possible seizure, then bleeding from everywhere including old puncture sites. Care is airway, oxygen, CPR if needed, left displacement, immediate transport.

cards.front: What is the field management of preterm labor?
cards.back: Left lateral position, oxygen if saturations are low, nothing in the vagina, no pushing, keep her warm and calm, and transport to a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit with early notification.

cards.front: What four questions do you ask before an imminent delivery?
cards.back: How many weeks, how many babies, was the fluid clear, and any known problems. Then warm the compartment to about 78 F, open towels and a hat, and start a clock at birth.

cards.front: What does MR SOPA stand for and when do you use it?
cards.back: Mask adjust, Reposition head, Suction mouth and nose, Open the mouth, Pressure increase, Airway alternative. Use it whenever ventilation is not making the chest rise, before adding compressions.

cards.front: What are the preductal SpO2 targets by minute of life?
cards.back: 1 minute 60 to 65 percent, 2 minutes 65 to 70, 3 minutes 70 to 75, 4 minutes 75 to 80, 5 minutes 80 to 85, and 10 minutes 85 to 95. Measure on the right hand.

cards.front: Which oxygen concentration do you start with in newborn ventilation?
cards.back: Room air for a term newborn, 21 to 30 percent for a preterm newborn if you can blend. Go to 100 percent only when chest compressions begin.

cards.front: How do you manage thermal care for a newborn under 32 weeks?
cards.back: Do not dry the body. Place directly into a food-grade plastic bag or wrap in plastic to the neck, dry only the head, add a hat, and target 36.5 to 37.5 C.

cards.front: What is the single best sign that newborn ventilation is working?
cards.back: A rising heart rate. Check it at the base of the cord or over the chest for 6 seconds and multiply by 10, and reassess every 30 seconds.

cards.front: List the common mechanical failures in neonatal resuscitation.
cards.back: Mask leak, a flexed or over-extended neck, bagging faster than 40 to 60 per minute, starting compressions before 30 seconds of effective ventilation, a cold compartment, and no hat.

cards.front: What five questions make up a fall workup in an older patient?
cards.back: What were you doing, do you remember hitting the ground, what happened right before, any new medication in 2 weeks, and how long were you down.

cards.front: What does a long lie on the floor add to a fall patient's problems?
cards.back: Over an hour brings hypothermia, dehydration, pressure injury to skin, and rhabdomyolysis that can damage the kidneys. Dark tea-colored urine is a clue worth reporting.

cards.front: How is orthostatic hypotension defined numerically?
cards.back: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, or a heart rate rise over 20. It is usually caused by a medication.

cards.front: What are the signs of a hip fracture after a fall?
cards.back: Groin or hip pain, the leg shortened and rotated outward, and inability to bear weight. Some patients still walk on a fractured hip, so pain alone justifies transport.

cards.front: Which form of delirium gets missed most often?
cards.back: The quiet, hypoactive form: withdrawn, slow and sleepy. It is written off as dementia or depression while an infection, low sodium or drug effect goes untreated.

cards.front: Why must a sulfonylurea hypoglycemia patient be transported?
cards.back: Glipizide and glyburide keep stimulating insulin for 12 to 24 hours. Oral glucose fixes the moment, not the cause, and the patient will drop again, often unobserved.

cards.front: What are the signs of digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Nausea and vomiting, yellow-green halos around lights, confusion, and a slow or irregular pulse. Levels climb as kidney function declines or a diuretic lowers potassium.

cards.front: What behavioral pattern suggests elder abuse or neglect?
cards.back: A caregiver who will not leave the room and answers questions asked of the patient, a patient who checks the caregiver's face before speaking, unfilled prescriptions, weight loss, pressure ulcers, and bruises in several stages of healing.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old with known asthma has been working hard for 25 minutes. His wheeze has become faint, he is drowsy, and SpO2 is 88% on a nonrebreather. Which finding most indicates impending respiratory arrest?
choices: Loud wheezing throughout exhalation
The chest becoming quiet while he remains drowsy and working
A respiratory rate of 34
Tremor and tachycardia after albuterol
quiz.why: A quiet chest means no air movement, and drowsiness means carbon dioxide is climbing. Loud wheezing actually proves air is still moving, and tremor with tachycardia is an expected albuterol effect.

quiz.q: A 7-month-old in January has had three days of runny nose and now wheezes with fine crackles and nasal congestion. This is his first wheezing episode. What is the most useful initial intervention?
choices: Suction the nose, give oxygen, and keep the head elevated
Give an epinephrine auto-injector
Lay him supine for better auscultation
Withhold oxygen so his drive to breathe is preserved
quiz.why: This is bronchiolitis, a plugging disease in a nose-dependent infant, so nasal suction changes his work of breathing more than anything else. Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis, supine worsens breathing, and the hypoxic drive concern does not apply here.

quiz.q: Which feature best distinguishes bronchiolitis from asthma?
choices: The presence of wheezing
A response to albuterol every time
Age under 2 with a first wheezing episode after several days of upper respiratory symptoms
Fever above 102 F
quiz.why: Both wheeze. Bronchiolitis is defined by young age, a first or second episode, and a viral prodrome, and it often does not respond to albuterol because the problem is plugging rather than spasm.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old asthmatic had a respiratory rate of 46 on your arrival. After one nebulizer treatment the rate is 22, he is harder to rouse, and SpO2 is unchanged at 90%. What is your interpretation?
choices: He responded well and can be transported without further treatment
The pulse oximeter is inaccurate because he is moving less
He needs a second nebulizer and nothing more
He is tiring and heading into respiratory failure, and needs assisted ventilation
quiz.why: A falling rate without a rising saturation and with worsening mental status means exhaustion, not improvement. A second treatment alone does not fix a child who has stopped moving air; assist ventilations and get ALS.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old has had a barking cough for two days. Tonight he has a temperature of 103.4 F, looks toxic, and his stridor worsened despite nebulized epinephrine at an urgent care. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Severe viral croup
Anaphylaxis
Bacterial tracheitis
Asthma exacerbation
quiz.why: Croup that deteriorates into a high fever with a toxic appearance and no response to nebulized epinephrine is bacterial tracheitis, which needs an operating room. Croup improves with epinephrine, anaphylaxis has hives and an exposure, and asthma causes expiratory wheeze rather than stridor.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old suddenly went silent while eating grapes. She is limp-handed, making no sound, and has blue lips. What do you do?
choices: Abdominal thrusts until the grape is expelled
Five back slaps with the head lower than the body, then five chest thrusts
A finger sweep of the mouth
Immediate CPR compressions while she is still responsive
quiz.why: For an infant with a complete obstruction, alternating five back slaps and five chest thrusts is the technique; abdominal thrusts risk the exposed liver. Blind sweeps push objects deeper, and CPR begins only when she becomes unresponsive.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old aspirated a peanut and is coughing forcefully, crying loudly, and pink, with occasional stridor between coughs. What is the correct management?
choices: Encourage coughing, position of comfort, oxygen as tolerated, and transport
Five abdominal thrusts immediately
Back blows until the peanut is expelled
Lay her flat and inspect the airway with a tongue depressor
quiz.why: Forceful coughing and crying prove good air exchange, and intervention can convert a partial obstruction into a complete one. Inspecting the airway risks spasm, and any sudden silence is your cue to act.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old choking on a piece of hot dog becomes unresponsive and slumps to the floor. What is your next action?
choices: Continue abdominal thrusts on the ground
Perform a blind finger sweep and then ventilate
Check a pulse for 30 seconds before deciding
Begin CPR with compressions, checking the mouth before each rescue breath
quiz.why: Chest compressions produce higher airway pressure than abdominal thrusts and may dislodge the object. Look in the mouth each time you open the airway and remove only what you can see; blind sweeps push objects past the cords.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old weighing 12 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days. HR 172, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool mottled legs, lethargic, BP 86/52. How do you classify him?
choices: Stable, since the blood pressure is normal for age
Compensated shock that is already severe
Decompensated shock requiring compressions
Simple viral illness with mild dehydration
quiz.why: The systolic is still above 70 plus twice the age, so he is compensating, but heart rate, refill and mental status say shock now. Compressions are for arrest, and mild dehydration does not produce mottling or lethargy.

quiz.q: Approximately how much total blood volume does a 20 kg child have?
choices: About 700 mL
About 1,000 mL
About 1,500 mL
About 2,800 mL
quiz.why: Children carry roughly 75 mL/kg, so 20 kg times 75 is about 1,500 mL. That is why a 300 mL loss represents 20 percent of volume and a scalp laceration can be life-threatening.

quiz.q: A 5-month-old is pale and feeding poorly with a regular heart rate of 268 that does not vary with stimulation. There is no fever and no history of illness. What is most likely?
choices: Sinus tachycardia from dehydration
Fever-related tachycardia
Supraventricular tachycardia causing cardiogenic shock
Normal infant heart rate
